articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities, Issues New General Licenses, and Amends FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued new general licenses pertaining to Iran and Russia, and amended existing Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs).
The action also included the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions enforcement in these regions.
Further details regarding the specific entities designated and the scope of the new general licenses are available on the Treasury Department's website.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations on Chinese Entities, Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations target Chinese entities, citing concerns over the theft of trade secrets.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated general licenses to guide compliance and mitigate unintended consequences. China's Ministry of Commerce has urged the U.S. to lift these sanctions, warning of countermeasures.
This action reflects the ongoing U.S. focus on intellectual property protection and national security concerns related to Chinese technological advancements.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) on October 16, 2026. This amendment, General License 60A, extends the authorization for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela until April 21, 2027.

This action supersedes the previous General License 60, providing an extended period for humanitarian aid and recovery operations in the country. The accompanying FAQ has been updated to reflect this extended authorization.
The amendment signals a continued, albeit specific, allowance for certain transactions amidst the broader sanctions framework targeting Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iranian Entities and a Cuban Entity, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation on October 15, 2026. This action also included the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The State Department sanctioned Banco Internacional de Comercio, S.A. (BICSA), a Cuban state-owned bank, for providing services to Karafarin Bank, an Iranian financial institution previously sanctioned by the U.S.
These designations and accompanying guidance reflect the U.S. government's continued focus on financial links between Cuba and Iran, and broader efforts to counter illicit financial activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan Politician Jorge Rodriguez from Sanctions List
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of Jorge Rodriguez, a prominent Venezuelan politician, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list on October 14, 2026.

Rodriguez, who serves as the President of Venezuela's National Assembly, was initially designated in 2018. His delisting ends the associated asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons engaging with him.
This action is part of a broader U.S. diplomatic push and an expansion of energy investment in Venezuela.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Al Jazeera / Steptoe

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Actions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism designations on October 13, 2026. This action targeted four individuals and eleven entities allegedly linked to the Cartel del Noreste (CDN), a Mexico-based cartel.
The CDN has been designated as both a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist. This marks OFAC's largest sanctions action to date against the CDN.
The designations were imposed pursuant to Executive Order 14059, which targets the international proliferation of illicit drugs and their means of production, and other relevant authorities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues International Criminal Court Designation and General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an International Criminal Court (ICC) designation and issued associated General Licenses on October 9, 2026. This action also included a Burma-related designation removal.
Further details regarding the specific nature of the ICC designation and the scope of the new general licenses are available on the Treasury Department's website.
This move indicates OFAC's continued engagement with international legal bodies and its dynamic approach to sanctions programs.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a new Russia-related General License on October 9, 2026. This General License 135 authorizes certain transactions related to imports of Russian diesel fuel to the U.S. until April 7, 2027.
This action follows President Trump's decision to waive the majority of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs introduced by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026.
The issuance of this General License suggests a strategic move to manage energy prices while navigating the broader sanctions landscape against Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes Iran-Related Designations, Issues New Iran and Amended Russia General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 8, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC issued a new Iran-related General License and an amended Russia-related General License.
These actions are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which targets Iran's shadow fleet network and aims to financially isolate the country.
The amended Russia-related General License further adjusts the U.S. sanctions posture concerning Russia, following recent developments in the broader sanctions framework.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State / Steptoe

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: The European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia on October 12, 2026, in response to Russia's continued aggression against Ukraine.
This package is primarily a listings package, adding 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals.

The measures specifically target companies forming the 'core' of Russia's military-industrial ecosystem, including those involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Hill Dickinson / Clyde & Co

articles.headline: EU Imposes New Sanctions on North Korea Over Nuclear Programs and Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on October 12, 2026.

These designations target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia and the 'arms-for-oil' trade.
The EU remains committed to the full implementation of UN sanctions against the DPRK and calls on North Korea to abandon its nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Consilium.europa.eu / NK PRO

articles.headline: EU Designates Individuals and Entities for Sanctions Circumvention and Illicit Trade with Russia
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures on October 15, 2026, targeting three individuals and nine entities involved in the import of sanctioned goods to Russia and the circumvention of EU sanctions related to oil and financial transactions.
These listings were adopted under the EU's restrictive measures framework concerning actions undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence.
Those designated are subject to an asset freeze and a prohibition on making funds or economic resources available to them, with listed individuals also facing an EU travel ban.

articles.headline: Cuba Accuses U.S. of Threatening Nations Ahead of UN Embargo Vote
body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures to pressure them into voting against an upcoming United Nations resolution.
The resolution calls for an end to the long-running U.S. economic embargo against the island, which has been in place for more than six decades.
Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Washington's ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, are personally leading the campaign to influence votes.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A., imposing a civil monetary penalty of $11,662,930.
This penalty is part of a larger enforcement action by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the OCC, totaling over $1.21 billion.

The violations stemmed from deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA)/anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program, including failures to properly monitor transactions and timely file suspicious activity reports.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / OCC.gov / U.S. Department of the Treasury

articles.headline: FCC Implements New Rule Blocking Drone Components from Covered List Companies
body: Effective October 13, 2026, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) will not authorize new devices, including U.S.-assembled drones, that contain logic-bearing parts made by companies on its Covered List, such as DJI or Autel.

This new rule, published in the Federal Register as FCC 26-50, targets companies building drones in the U.S. and aims to close a loophole that previously allowed the use of components from listed entities.
While existing DJI aircraft remain legal to fly and previously authorized models can still be sold, this action significantly impacts the future market for new drone models and components in the U.S.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
